question: How does whale oil become an industry, and how do the Reformation and the Atlantic reshuffle the fats of Europe and the world?
summary: Whale oil comes first. The Basques' station at Red Bay in Labrador (about 1536), Muscovy Company ships and Basque harpooners at Spitsbergen in 1611, and the Dutch fleet that grows from 30–40 ships in 1642 to 178 in 1670 turn whaling into a state-backed industry, fought over by the English and the Dutch ([[ec1]], [[ec2]], [[c1]], [[o1]], [[o3]]). Soap-boilers finance voyages and colonial towns regulate drift whales ([[ec3]], [[o4]]), while London's tallow chandlers cannot make enough candles ([[ec8]]).

The Reformation turns the fat line into politics: Luther rails at the Lenten oil and the sale of butter, while the Cardinal of Aragon travels with his own oil to avoid butter's leprosy ([[b1]], [[th1]], [[e1]]); butter becomes a status symbol even in Italy, and the Dutch become ‘butterboxes’ ([[ec7]], [[ec5]]).

The Atlantic and Asia carry oil in other directions. Palm oil moves from Angola and São Tomé to Brazil and seasons the gruel on slave ships ([[ec4]], [[l1]]); the olive is planted in the Americas ([[x1]]); Britain hopes sesame will replace imported olive oil, and Africans bring *benne* to the American South ([[ec6]]); and in China Song Yingxing ranks the oils and describes the Ming press ([[th3]], [[te1]]).

themes.title: Whaling as a state industry
text: From a Labrador station to a monopoly, a war and customs duties: the oil of the right whale lights and soaps Europe.

themes.title: Butter and oil after Luther
text: A moral and medical geography in which butter-eating countries turn Protestant, the Dutch dairy economy flourishes and southern butter becomes a luxury.

themes.title: The Atlantic's fats
text: Palm oil on slave ships, sesame as a colonial hope, olive trees in the missions.

themes.title: Light, soap and tallow
text: A pre-industrial city runs on tallow candles and soap-boilers' oil; the courts burn wax by the thousand.

themes.title: Ming China's oils
text: A ranking of oils by use, and a press that remains unchanged to the twentieth century.

turning_points.text: Luther attacks the Lenten oil and the sale of butter.
Red Bay becomes the Basques' whale-oil station in Labrador.
The first whale is killed at Spitsbergen, by a Basque harpooner.
Song Yingxing ranks the oils and describes the press.
The Mortamer ledger shows palm oil crossing to Brazil.
England's Navigation Act aims to restrict Dutch whale oil.

how_to_read: The whale entries are the longest connected chain; follow them through *Economy*, *Order* and *Conflict*. *Belief* and *Thought* carry the Reformation fat line.
The Nexus shows how the whaling rivalry and the soap trade connect.

sources.intro: Ellis's whaling history and Dolin's American whaling carry the industry; Khosrova, Flandrin and Mueller the butter and oil politics; Zuckerman and Lynn the palm oil; Needham the Chinese side.
main: Khosrova, Flandrin and Mueller ([[b1]], [[th1]], [[e1]], [[ec5]], [[ec7]], [[o2]]); Kiple for the sunflower, coconut and sesame ([[th2]], [[ec9]], [[ec6]]).
Zuckerman and Lynn for palm oil ([[ec4]], [[l1]]); Needham for China ([[th3]], [[te1]]); Lowengard for tallow ([[ec8]]); Schivelbusch for Versailles ([[e2]]).
contested: Flandrin's idea that oil-hatred helped drive the Reformation ([[b1]]).
The 1618 soap-oil fines are reported without the order ([[o2]]).
Palm oil on the slave ship rests on a popular history with period examples ([[l1]]).
gaps: No source for Mexican and Peruvian oil production under Spanish rule; none for Indian fats in the Mughal period.
Dutch and Danish primary records of whaling and the Hamburg trade were not read.
